did.abstract: The Butcher and Johnson families papers, circa 1910-2025, document the lives of Alexander Butcher and his daughter Ina Johnson and their families who moved from Barbados, to Panama, Cuba, New Orleans, LA, and finally settled in the Bedford-Stuyvesant neighborhood in Brooklyn in the 1920s. The papers include correspondence, photographs, passports, birth and baptismal certificates, citizenship papers, papers related to home ownership, and ephemera related to churches, schools, civic organizations, concerts, and dances.
did.langmaterial: Materials primarily in English, with some documents in Spanish.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The Butcher and Johnson families papers, circa 1910-2025, document the lives of Alexander Butcher and his daughter Ina Johnson and their families who settled in the Bedford-Stuyvesant neighborhood of Brooklyn after emigrating from Barbados to Panama, Cuba, and New Orleans, LA. Materials in the collection include correspondence, identification and citizenship documents, property ownership paperwork, photographs, and ephemera related to church activities, performances, and schools.

Most of the material is related to the families' lives in Brooklyn with some identification documents and birth certificates from Barbados and Cuba. While Series 5 is devoted to photographs, there are photographs present throughout the other series.

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Alexander Butcher (1888?-1988) was born in Barbados, then moved to Panama looking for work where he met and married Maud Spence (1899-1924). The couple moved to Cuba and then New Orleans, Louisiana. Maud Spence Butcher died in 1924 in New Orleans and Alexander Butcher brought their three children to Brooklyn. Butcher worked as a carpenter and shipwright and was active in the First AME Zion Church on MacDonough Street.

One of Alexander Butcher's sisters, Dessymonia (also known as Desdemona and Justeena) A. D. Swain (1889-1964) moved to Panama in 1926 with her daughter Mary R. Swain. In 1927, they both moved to New York and settled in Brooklyn.

Swain's daughter, Mary Rosalien Swain (b. 1912), immigrated to New York with her mother in 1927. She graduated from Girls' Commercial High School in 1938 and worked for the federal government in the Bureau of International Organization Affairs.

Ina Louise Butcher (1921-2025), Alexander Butcher's oldest daughter, was born in Cuba and grew up mostly in Brooklyn. She married Booker T. Johnson (1906-1987) from Union, South Carolina in 1943. The couple had ten children and raised them in Bedford-Stuyvesant. Ina Johnson worked as a stenographer and secretary and was active in the Our Lady of Good Counsel Roman Catholic Church.
More detailed biographical information is available on the series level.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: This collection is organized into five series:
- Series 1: Alexander and Maud Spence Butcher papers, circa 1910-1988
- Series 2: Dessymonia A. D. Swain papers, 1926-1961
- Series 4: Ina and Booker T. Johnson papers, 1921-2025

did.unittitle: Series 1: Alexander and Maud Spence Butcher papers

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Series 1: Alexander and Maud Spence Butcher papers, circa 1910-1988, consists of records related to the lives and work of Alexander and Maud Spence Butcher. Types of materials include correspondence, notebooks, citizenship and identification papers, ephemera related to church and organizational memberships, and paperwork related to renting and purchasing property in Brooklyn.

Alexander Butcher's Panama Canal employment records include applications for retirement benefits. His shipwright employment records include details of an incident of discrimination at the Brooklyn Navy Yard.

Certificates of Black Star Line stock and Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA) membership from New Orleans indicate Alexander Butcher's support of Pan-Africanism. Publications in the folder of Black liberation readings include Reverend Herbert Daughtry's "Seize the Future" (1979), "Onward, Jamaica!" from the Jamaica Progressive League of New York (1937), and "A Negro Looks at War" by John Henry Williams (1940).
Correspondence from 1923 to 1925 gives insight into the family's life in New Orleans, Maud's death, and caring for the children after her death.

Alexander Butcher wrote several affidavits of support for relatives coming from Barbados and Panama, which include information about Alexander Butcher's employment, salary, and address at the time. Folders titled with addresses are homes Alexander Butcher rented or bought and include rent receipts, letters to tenants, and deeds.

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Alexander Butcher was born in Barbados on June 4, 1892 (according to his passport) or June 13, 1893 (according to his naturalization papers) or January 16, 1888 (according to a resolution from the Consulate General of Barbados on his 99th birthday) to John Butcher and Mary Archer Butcher.

Alexander Butcher left home when he was 12 years old to earn money for his family. He immigrated to Panama in 1906 and worked as a carpenter on the Panama Canal. Butcher met Maud Spence in Panama. Maud (also spelled Maude) Carmen Spence was born August 28, 1899 in Panama City, Panama to Rebeca Gable and Alfred Spence. Maud and Alexander moved to Cuba after the 1920 Panama Canal workers strike and married on November 8, 1922 at the Holy Trinity Cathedral in Havana, Cuba. The Butchers had four children: Lloyd Franklin (1918- circa 1918), George Earl (Ernest) (1920-1996), Ina Louise (1921-2025), and Laura (1923-1991).

The family moved to New Orleans, LA in 1923. Alexander Butcher moved to Brooklyn in 1924 and first lived at 485 Herkimer Street, planning to send for Maud and the children once he was settled. However, Maud Butcher died July 17, 1924 in New Orleans, LA and the children moved to New York City.

In 1928, Alexander Butcher became a naturalized citizen. He and his three children were living at 162 Jefferson Avenue in Brooklyn at that time. Alexander Butcher worked as a carpenter and was employed by the Brooklyn Navy Yard. He was a member of the United Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners of America and was active in the First AME Zion Church at 54 MacDonough Street. Alexander Butcher owned several properties in Brooklyn: 113 Hancock Street, 565 Halsey Street, and 80 Kingston Avenue.

did.unittitle: Series 2: Dessymonia A. D. Swain papers

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Series 2: Dessymonia A. D. Swain papers, 1926-1961, includes the papers of one of Alexander Butcher's sisters. Materials include her passport, music books of Christian hymns and songs, possibly collected at churches in New York City, and correspondence from her sister Victoria Morgan (also known as Aunt Pritty or Aunt Pretty) in Barbados. The passport also includes a picture of Swain's daughter, Mary R. Swain.

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Dessymonia Aurora Delphenice Swain (née Butcher) was born August 31, 1889 in Barbados to John Butcher and Mary Archer Butcher. She is the sister of Alexander Butcher. After she was widowed, she moved to Panama with her daughter Mary R. Swain in 1926 and soon the United States in 1927. She arrived in New York on June 15, 1927 on the ship Mongolia. She was also known as Desdemona or Jestene or Justeena. She became a citizen of the United States in 1939 and died in 1964.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Series 3: Mary Swain papers, 1927-1970, includes materials related to Mary R. Swain, Alexander Butcher's niece and Ina Johnson's first cousin. Materials related to her career in the federal government include a photograph with President Richard Nixon, a U.S. Department of State publication about the SALT (Strategic Arms Limitation Talks) process, and applications for going on leave during an illness in the 1960s. Correspondence from the Caribbean is mostly from her aunt Victoria Morgan (also known as Aunt Pritty or Aunt Pretty) and her family in Barbados and a Christian mission she supported in Suriname.

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Mary Rosalien Swain was born on December 12, 1912. She immigrated to New York with her mother Dessymonia A. D. Swain in 1927 and they settled in Brooklyn. She graduated from Girls' Commercial High School at Classon Avenue and Union Street in 1938. Mary Swain worked for the Bureau of International Organization Affairs and spent some time living and working in Washington, DC.

Series 4: Ina and Booker T. Johnson papers

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Ina Butcher was born on July 21, 1921 in Havana, Cuba to Alexander and Maud Butcher. Soon after, the Butchers moved to New Orleans, LA and then New York after Maud Butcher died. She and her siblings stayed with different family members in Manhattan and Brooklyn as Alexander Butcher looked for work. She attended P.S. 3 and P.S. 4 in Brooklyn. She went to Julia Ward Howe Junior High School (J.H.S. 81) and Wadleigh High School in Harlem, Manhattan. She graduated from Haaren High School on 10th Avenue in Manhattan in 1940.

After graduating from high school, Ina worked as a stenographer for the National Youth Administration and moved to Washington, DC to work for the Chief of Finance. However, the death of her friend, Maude Wilson, brought her back to New York where she lived with her friend's family at 98 Morningside Avenue.

While working at the Brooklyn Navy Yard, Ina met Booker T. Johnson and they married on November 23, 1943 at St. Martin's Episcopal Church in Harlem. Booker Telifero Johnson was born on October 20, 1906 in Union, South Carolina to Frank Jordan Johnson and Julia Gleen Johnson. He was the oldest of eleven siblings. Booker T. Johnson worked as a tractor trailer driver and a cab driver.

Ina and Booker T. Johnson had ten children: Elliot (1944-2016), Douglas (also known as Krip) (1946-2019), Adele (1947- ), Margaret (1949- ), Monica (1952- ), Valerie (1953- ), Genevieve (1954- ), Orlando (1954- ), Pamela (1957- ), and Randolph (1957- ). In 1949, the family moved to the Marcy Houses at 123 Nostrand Avenue. In 1967, Johnson bought 571 Decatur Street. Most of the children attended the St. Ambrose Church School at 222 Tompkins Avenue.

In 1964, Ina returned to her work as a stenographer at the State of New York Banking Department and in the late 1970s, she began working as a secretary at Boys and Girls High School on Fulton Street. She retired in 1986. Booker T. Johnson died on November 25, 1987.

In 1974, she received her associate's degree in secretarial sciences from New York City Community College. She received two degrees from Brooklyn College: a bachelor's degree in African Studies in 1983 and a master's in History in 2003.

She was an active member of Our Lady of Good Counsel Roman Catholic Church. She was a member of the 500 Decatur Street Block Association and served on the 81st Precinct Community Council. Ina Johnson was involved with the group Sisters Against South African Apartheid (SASAA) and was arrested at a protest against the murder of Amadou Diallo on March 23, 1999. Ina Johnson died on January 30, 2025.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Series 4: Ina Butcher and Booker T. Johnson papers, 1921-2025, includes materials related to the family, work, education, and activities of Ina and Booker T. Johnson. Types of materials include correspondence, notebooks, photographs, programs, greeting cards and invitations, certificates, and passports and other forms of identification.

This series includes materials related to Brooklyn schools and the Johnsons' education. There are report cards for Ina and her ten children. The children's report cards are usually accompanied by a graduation program or other school activity ephemera. Ina's papers she wrote for her bachelor's and master's degrees at Brooklyn College, written from 1994 to 2003, are also included.

Materials from Ina Johnson's late high school/post-high school years include invitations to dances in Harlem sponsored by the Union Boys and other organizations. Venues include the Renaissance Casino, Lido Ballroom, Criterion Studio, and the Congress Casino.

Ina Johnson's creative and civic activities are well-documented in this series. Creative pursuits are shown through sewing patterns, collected poetry and prose, and a scrapbook of clippings from the recurring newspaper section "Poems You Ought to Know," and work from a calligraphy workshop. The folder titled "Politics - Police" includes Ina Johnson's account of her arrest with Reverends Al Sharpton and Herbert Daughtry at a protest against the murder of Amadou Diallo on March 23, 1999.
Ina Johnson's budget notepads in this series, dated 1977 to 2000, document income and expenses with some receipts and small notes tucked into the pages.

Also included are several issues of the Johnson Family News and Johnson Family Financial News sent out to family members to provide updates and teach younger members of the family financial literacy. The Johnson children and grandchildren also created two Kwanzaa books for Ina Johnson that are included in this series and contain artwork and historical writings.

Butcher and Johnson family histories and genealogy are included in Ina Johnson's 75th birthday celebration booklet (produced in 1996) and the memorial books for Ina and Booker T. Johnson (both produced in 2025).

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Series 5: Photographs, circa 1910-2016, includes studio portraits and candid photographs of the Butcher and Johnson families in Barbados, Brooklyn, and Washington, DC. The bulk of the series is made up of photographs of Ina Johnson, Booker T. Johnson, and their children. The earlier photographs depict Alexander Butcher, his siblings, and children.

Photographs of the Johnson children depict them outside at the Marcy Houses, dressed for graduation or confirmation ceremonies, and in baby or graduation portraits. Photographs of Genevieve Johnson show her with a Fresh Air Fund host family in Chappaqua, New York in the 1960s. Photographs from Barbados, circa 1980, depict Peter (Alexander Butcher's half brother) and his family. The photographs of the Johnson family reunion in Washington, DC in 2016 are printed in a book.
